title: Niu Leads UCF Effort To Cut Quantum Computing Costs
excerpt: UCF researcher Niu is working with her research team to determine if a partially fault-tolerant quantum computer can offer a workable middle ground between today’s noisy devices and fully fault-tolerant machines.
content:
A $400,000 grant from the Department of Energy is funding research at the University of Central Florida to explore a compromise between error-prone quantum computers and the costly pursuit of full fault tolerance. Assistant Professor Siyuan Niu and her team, including co-investigators Di Wu and Eduardo Mucciolo, are developing software tools to assess the viability of quantum computers by simulating electron behavior in materials.

“For this project, the task is simulating how electrons behave in materials,” Niu says, with the ultimate goal of determining if these machines can achieve practical quantum utility. The team will deliver an open-source framework to estimate the resources needed for these simulations.

Fermi-Hubbard Model Benchmarks for Partially Fault-Tolerant Quantum Computing

The University of Central Florida team led by Siyuan Niu is focusing on the Space-Time Efficient Analog Rotation, or STAR, architecture as a means of reducing the overhead associated with quantum error correction. This partially fault-tolerant design employs full error correction for fundamental quantum operations, but applies computationally intensive rotation operations, critical for material simulations, directly with limited protection. This approach, Niu explains, “could avoid some of the extra qubits and time required by fully fault-tolerant designs to perform such rotations,” offering a potential shortcut to practical quantum computation.

The team’s compiler and resource estimations are being specifically tailored to manage the inherent trade-offs of this partial protection strategy. A key challenge lies in the management of residual errors within these analog rotations; these operations may require repetition until successful completion.

The project’s framework will not only estimate the resources needed for simulations but also account for the scheduling and management of these potentially iterative steps. By the project’s conclusion, the team intends to deliver an open-source framework combining a quantum simulation compiler, a GPU-based decoder, and a resource estimator, allowing researchers to assess the quantum and classical computing demands of electron simulations.

This modular design will allow other research groups to integrate their own decoding and compilation methods, encouraging wider collaboration and innovation. The team’s benchmark for evaluating this approach is the Fermi-Hubbard model, a widely used method for studying interacting electrons in materials.

The goal is to determine if a partially fault-tolerant computer can accurately simulate the evolution of these electrons over time while effectively managing errors. “Quantum computers need this because qubits are fragile, and errors accumulate during the many operations a useful simulation requires,” Niu says, highlighting the fundamental need for error mitigation in any practical quantum computation. The system will spread information across multiple physical qubits, repeatedly checking for errors and using a fast decoder to correct them before they compromise the results.

The broader objective extends beyond simply achieving a successful simulation. The team aims to establish a clear understanding of when these advanced machines can deliver results at a reasonable cost. Niu’s team is working to define the point at which quantum computers can perform scientifically valuable computations. “Comparing those results with today’s noisy, unprotected devices and fully protected designs could help researchers decide which simulations are realistic, which hardware improvements matter most and when useful applications might become feasible,” Niu says.

The resulting framework will be a roadmap and assessment tool, rather than a guaranteed demonstration of quantum advantage, providing valuable insights into the viability of partially fault-tolerant quantum computing. The ultimate aim is to determine if this middle-ground approach, less demanding than full fault tolerance but more robust than current noisy devices, can allow for the development of quantum computing for materials science and beyond.
